## Overview

Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate. Rather than allowing an unbounded buffer to grow until the process runs out of memory, backpressure ensures that producers pace themselves according to the consumer's ability to process data.

## Common Implementations

Backpressure can be implemented through several established patterns:

### Bounded Queues

The producer writes to a queue with a fixed maximum capacity. Once the queue reaches its limit, further write operations block the producer until the consumer drains enough items to make space. This provides a natural throttling mechanism and prevents memory exhaustion.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

In this model, the consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send a specific number of items (credits). The producer may only emit up to the granted credit limit. As the consumer processes items, it returns credits or grants new ones, allowing the producer to resume emission. This gives the consumer fine-grained control over the emission rate.

### Reactive-Pull Models

Instead of the producer pushing items at its own pace, the consumer requests items on its own schedule. The producer only emits when explicitly asked, which naturally enforces backpressure since emission is demand-driven rather than supply-driven. This is the fundamental model underlying reactive programming frameworks.

## Significance

Backpressure is critical for building robust, memory-efficient streaming systems. Without it, a mismatch between producer and consumer rates can lead to unbounded memory growth, system instability, or crashes. Proper backpressure handling is a cornerstone of [[reactive-systems]] design.
